newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. sanctions against Libya unchanged after review.
newsitem.headline: U.N. sanctions against Libya unchanged after review.

text.p: The Security Council on Friday brushed aside claims that Lybia had complied with demands related to the 1988 bombing of a Pan Am airliner over Scotland and left unchanged U.N. sanctions imposed five years ago.

The decision, announced by council President Zbigniew Wlosowicz of Poland, followed a periodic 120-day review of the sanctions, which include an air embargo, a ban on arms sales and the downgrading of diplomatic relations.

They were first enacted in 1992 because of Libya's failure to extradite to Britain or the United States two alleged intelligence officers indicted in both countries on charges of planting a bomb aboard Pan Am flight 103, which exploded over the Scottish village of Lockerbie killing 270 people, including 11 on the ground.
The sanctions also penalized Libya for not cooperating in the investigation into the 1989 bombing of a French UTA airliner over Niger which killed all 171 people aboard.

The curbs were toughened in 1993 to include a freeze on some of Libya's assets abroad and a ban on its import of certain types of equipment used in oil terminals and refineries. They do not affect the export of oil from Libya or its purchase of oil drilling equipment.
The Organization of African Unity and the Arab League recently told the Security Council that Libya had fully met its demands.

They said that while Libya was unable to extradite the two suspects to Britain or the United States for trial, it was willing for them to be tried in a neutral country to be determined by the Security Council. Alternatively, they could be tried by Scottish judges under Scottish law at the seat of the World Court at The Hague or by a special criminal tribunal to be established there.

American U.N. ambassador Bill Richardson told council colleagues during the review that, apart from not surrendering the two men for trial by a British or U.S. court, Libya had not fully cooperated in the investigations into the two bombings, had not paid appropriate compensation and had "not ceased its support for terrorism."
"This does not look like full compliance to me or my government," Richardson said.

He also said a Libyan aircraft violated sanctions in January by flying an official delegation to Accra, Ghana, and had yet to respond to inquiries about the incident by the council's sanctions committee.

French deputy U.N. representative Herve Ladsous, whose remarks to the council were also made public, disclosed that a French magistrate who has been probing the UTA airliner bombing and visited Tripoli last July had received enough cooperation to make significant progress.

This opened the way for a trial of six suspects in absentia, which was possible under French law, he said. France hoped Libya would comply with all provisions of the council's resolutions so as to be able to regain its place in the international community as soon as possible, he added.
Ladsous did not say when the trial in absentia might begin or give details about the six suspects or their whereabouts.
